+# Update the Defender for SQL extension manually - Microsoft Defender for Cloud | Microsoft Learn
+
+Update the Defender for SQL extension on an Azure Arc-enabled server or Azure virtual machine (VM) to the latest version available in the machine's Azure region. Choose the Azure portal procedure or the scripted procedure for your machine type, then verify the installed version and SQL Server protection status.
+
+These procedures target the extension with publisher `Microsoft.Azure.AzureDefenderForSQL` and type `AdvancedThreatProtection.Windows`. They don't update the SQL IaaS extension or the Azure Connected Machine agent.
+
+## Update by using the Azure portal
+
+Use the portal to inspect the installed extension and update to the latest offered version where an update action is available.
+
+### Update an Arc-enabled server
+
+1. In the Azure portal, open **Machines - Azure Arc**, and select the server that hosts SQL Server.
+2. Under **Settings**, select **Extensions**.
+3. Find the Defender for SQL extension by its publisher and type.
+4. Check **Update available** for the latest offered version.
+5. If an update is available, select the extension, and then select **Update**.
+6. Refresh the extension details and verify the resulting version and status.
+
+The [Arc portal upgrade procedure](/en-us/azure/azure-arc/servers/manage-vm-extensions-portal#upgrade-extensions) documents this update action. An Arc extension upgrade preserves its configuration.
+
+### Inspect and update an Azure VM
+
+1. In the Azure portal, open **Virtual machines**, and select the VM that hosts SQL Server.
+2. Under **Settings**, select **Extensions + applications**.
+3. Select the Defender for SQL extension and review its version and status.
+4. If an extension update action is available, use it to start the update. Otherwise, use the Azure VM CLI example.
+5. Refresh the extension details and verify the resulting version and status.
+
+The [Defender for SQL troubleshooting guidance](/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/troubleshoot-sql-machines-guide#step-3-identify-and-resolve-protection-misconfigurations-at-the-sql-server-instance-level) directs customers to update outdated extensions from the machine's extensions page.
+
+## Update programmatically
+
+Use Azure CLI to update the extension on an Arc-enabled server or Azure VM.
+
+### Prerequisites
+
+- An Azure Arc-enabled Windows server or Azure Windows VM with the Defender for SQL extension already installed. For initial setup, see [Enable Defender for SQL Servers on Machines](/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/defender-for-sql-usage).
+- Permission to read the machine and its extensions and perform the relevant update operation. For Arc-enabled servers, **Azure Connected Machine Resource Administrator** includes the extension upgrade permission. For Azure VMs, **Virtual Machine Contributor** includes extension management permissions. Scope permissions to the resources you manage, or use a custom role with the necessary actions. See the [Arc role definition](/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/built-in-roles/management-and-governance#azure-connected-machine-resource-administrator) and [VM role definition](/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/built-in-roles/compute#virtual-machine-contributor).
+- The network and extension deployment requirements in [Defender for SQL prerequisites](/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/defender-for-sql-usage#prerequisites).
+- For the scripted procedures, PowerShell 7 and the [Azure CLI](/en-us/cli/azure/install-azure-cli).
+- For the Arc procedure, Azure CLI version 2.75.0 or later and the `connectedmachine` CLI extension.
+- Before either CLI procedure, sign in with `az login` and select the subscription with `az account set --subscription "<subscription-id>"`.
+
+### Update an Arc-enabled server by using Azure CLI
+
+Run these commands in PowerShell for the Arc-enabled machine that hosts SQL Server. Replace the placeholders with your resource details. The update and verification examples use the extension resource name `MicrosoftDefenderForSQL`. If your installed extension has a different resource name, use that name instead.
+
+1. Update to the latest available version. This command enables minor-version selection at deployment and leaves future automatic upgrades enabled. The output includes the extension's status.
+
+    ```powershell
+    az connectedmachine extension update `
+      --resource-group "<resource-group>" `
+      --machine-name "<arc-machine-name>" `
+      --name "MicrosoftDefenderForSQL" `
+      --publisher "Microsoft.Azure.AzureDefenderForSQL" `
+      --type "AdvancedThreatProtection.Windows" `
+      --auto-upgrade-minor-version true `
+      --enable-auto-upgrade true
+    ```
+2. Verify the version and status if needed, or run this command later to check again. Confirm that the provisioning state is `Succeeded` and review the installed runtime version.
+
+    ```powershell
+    az connectedmachine extension show `
+        --resource-group "<resource-group>" `
+        --machine-name "<arc-machine-name>" `
+        --name "MicrosoftDefenderForSQL" `
+        --output json
+    ```
+
+For command details, see [Update an Arc machine extension](/en-us/cli/azure/connectedmachine/extension#az-connectedmachine-extension-update) and [Show an Arc machine extension](/en-us/cli/azure/connectedmachine/extension#az-connectedmachine-extension-show). For future automatic updates, see [Automatic extension upgrade for Azure Arc-enabled servers](/en-us/azure/azure-arc/servers/manage-automatic-vm-extension-upgrade).
+
+### Update an Azure VM by using Azure CLI
+
+Run these commands in PowerShell to update the existing Defender for SQL extension. Replace the placeholders with your resource details.
+
+Important
+
+The Azure VM command requests the `2.0` handler series, not a specific four-part build. Azure delivers the latest available patch/hotfix in that series.
+
+For the Arc proxy scenario, the required installed Defender for SQL build is `2.0.3585.403` or later. Requesting a handler series alone doesn't prove that the installed build meets this requirement.
+
+1. Update to the latest available version in the handler series. The command leaves future automatic upgrades enabled and returns the extension's status. `--force-update` requests an update even if the configuration hasn't changed.
+
+    ```powershell
+    az vm extension set `
+        --resource-group "<resource-group>" `
+        --vm-name "<vm-name>" `
+        --publisher "Microsoft.Azure.AzureDefenderForSQL" `
+        --name "AdvancedThreatProtection.Windows" `
+        --version "2.0" `
+        --enable-auto-upgrade true `
+        --force-update
+    ```
+2. Verify the version and status if needed, or run this command later to check again. Retrieve the extension's instance view, confirm that provisioning succeeded, and review the installed runtime version and any failure details.
+
+    ```powershell
+    az vm extension show `
+        --resource-group "<resource-group>" `
+        --vm-name "<vm-name>" `
+        --name "AdvancedThreatProtection.Windows" `
+        --instance-view `
+        --output json
+    ```
+
+For command details, see [Set a VM extension](/en-us/cli/azure/vm/extension#az-vm-extension-set) and [Show a VM extension](/en-us/cli/azure/vm/extension#az-vm-extension-show).
+
+## Verify the update and SQL Server protection
+
+Check the installed runtime version, not only the requested handler version.
+
+For Arc, inspect `properties.instanceView.typeHandlerVersion` in the REST representation, or the equivalent field returned by your CLI. For an Azure VM, inspect the instance view requested in the scripted procedure. Compare the reported installed build with the feature's required build. For the Arc proxy scenario, verify `2.0.3585.403` or later. A major/minor value alone doesn't establish the four-part installed build.
+
+To confirm SQL Server protection, open the relevant **SQL virtual machines** or **SQL Server - Azure Arc** resource in the portal. Under **Security**, select **Defender for Cloud**, and confirm that **Protection status** is **Protected**. If the update fails or protection isn't healthy, use [Troubleshoot Defender for SQL on machines configuration](/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/troubleshoot-sql-machines-guide).
+
+For the resource-level protection check, see [Verify SQL machine protection](/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/verify-machine-protection#verify-protection-on-a-single-sql-server-vm). The subscription recommendation refreshes every 12 hours, so don't use an immediate recommendation change as the only verification.
+
+## REST API reference
+
+For REST API integration, use these references.
+
+- [Arc machine extension Update API](/en-us/rest/api/hybridcompute/machine-extensions/update)
+- [Azure VM extension Update API](/en-us/rest/api/compute/virtual-machine-extensions/update)
+- [Azure VM extension Get API](/en-us/rest/api/compute/virtual-machine-extensions/get)
\ No newline at end of file

englishSummary.headline: New guidance for manually updating the Defender for SQL extension
englishSummary.summary: A new page explains how to update the Defender for SQL extension on Azure Arc-enabled servers and Azure VMs using the Azure portal, Azure CLI, scripts, or REST APIs. It also covers prerequisites, version verification, and the extensions in scope.
englishSummary.adminImpact: Administrators can use these procedures to keep the Defender for SQL extension current and verify its status without updating the SQL IaaS extension or Azure Connected Machine agent.

 If you have issues with Microsoft Defender for Endpoint on Linux and need support, you might be asked to provide the output from the Client Analyzer tool. It's a diagnostic tool that helps administrators and support teams troubleshoot issues with Microsoft Defender for Endpoint. It collects detailed information about installation, configuration, service health, logs, connectivity status, etc. This tool is primarily used for checking system health, validating configurations, and helping troubleshoot potential issues.
 
-This article explains how to use the tool on your device or with live response. You can use either a Python-based solution or a binary version that doesn't need Python.
+You can collect Client Analyzer diagnostics in any of the following ways:
+
+1. **Command line**: Run the Client Analyzer locally on the device. See run-the-binary-version-of-the-client-analyzer or run-the-python-based-client-analyzer.
+2. **Live response**: Run the Client Analyzer remotely during a live response session. See use-live-response-to-collect-diagnostics-log
+3. **Investigation package**: Collect an investigation package from the device page in the Microsoft Defender portal. On Linux, the package includes Client Analyzer diagnostics. See [collect-investigation-package-from-devices](/en-us/defender-endpoint/respond-machine-alerts)
 
 Tip

englishSummary.adminImpact: Administrators can use the documented collection method that best fits their investigation workflow; no configuration change is required.

@@ -555,177 +514,14 @@ Important
 
 Windows uses the carriage return and line feed invisible characters to represent the end of one line and beginning of a new line in a file. Linux systems use only the Line Feed invisible character at the end of file lines. When you use the following scripts, if done on Windows, this difference can result in errors and failures of the scripts to run. A potential solution to this is to utilize the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) and the `dos2unix` package to reformat the script so it aligns with the Unix and Linux format standard.
 
-#### Run Client Analyzer from the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint installation
-
-If Microsoft Defender for Endpoint is already installed on the device, you can run the Client Analyzer directly from the agent installation without downloading or installing additional packages.
-
-- Create an `MDESupportToolBinary.sh` file and paste the following content into it.
-
-    ```bash
-    #! /usr/bin/bash
-    
-    echo "cd /opt/microsoft/mdatp/tools/client_analyzer/binary"
-    cd /opt/microsoft/mdatp/tools/client_analyzer/binary
-    
-    echo "Running MDESupportTool"
-    ./MDESupportTool $@
-    
-    Execute:
-    run MDESupportToolBinary.sh -parameters "--bypass-disclaimer -d"
-
-    MDESupportToolPython.sh
-    
-    #! /usr/bin/bash
-    
-    echo "cd /opt/microsoft/mdatp/tools/client_analyzer/python"
-    cd /opt/microsoft/mdatp/tools/client_analyzer/python
-    
-    echo "Running MDESupportTool"
-    ./mde_support_tool.sh $@
-    
-    Execute:
-    run MDESupportToolPython.sh -parameters "--bypass-disclaimer -d"
-    
-    ```
-
-### Install the XMDE Client Analyzer
-
-Download and extract the XMDE Client Analyzer. You can use either the binary or Python version, as follows:
-
-- [Binary version of the Client Analyzer](run-analyzer-linux#run-the-binary-version-of-the-client-analyzer)
-- [Python version of the Client Analyzer](run-analyzer-linux#run-the-python-based-client-analyzer)
-
-Due to the limited commands available in live response, the steps detailed must be executed in a bash script. By splitting the installation and execution portion of these commands, it's possible to run the install script once, and run the execution script multiple times.
-
-Important
-
-The example scripts assume the machine has direct internet access and can retrieve the XMDE Client Analyzer from Microsoft. If the machine doesn't have direct internet access, then the installation scripts must be updated to fetch the XMDE Client Analyzer from a location the machines can access successfully.
-
-#### Binary client analyzer install script
-
-The following script performs the first six steps of the [Running the Binary version of the Client Analyzer](run-analyzer-linux#run-the-binary-version-of-the-client-analyzer). When complete, the XMDE Client Analyzer binary is available from the `/tmp/XMDEClientAnalyzerBinary/ClientAnalyzer` directory.
-
-- Create a bash file `InstallXMDEClientAnalyzer.sh` and paste the following content into it.
-
-    ```bash
-    #! /usr/bin/bash 
-    
-    echo "Starting Client Analyzer Script. Running As:"
-    whoami
-    
-    echo "Getting XMDEClientAnalyzerBinary"
-    wget --quiet -O /tmp/XMDEClientAnalyzerBinary.zip https://aka.ms/XMDEClientAnalyzerBinary
-    echo 'C65A4E4C6851D130942BFACD147A9D18B8A92B4F50FACF519477FD1C41A1C323 /tmp/XMDEClientAnalyzerBinary.zip' | sha256sum -c
-    
-    echo "Unzipping XMDEClientAnalyzerBinary.zip"
-    unzip -q /tmp/XMDEClientAnalyzerBinary.zip -d /tmp/XMDEClientAnalyzerBinary
-    
-    echo "Unzipping SupportToolLinuxBinary.zip"
-    unzip -q /tmp/XMDEClientAnalyzerBinary/XMDEClientAnalyzer/SupportToolLinuxBinary.zip -d /tmp/XMDEClientAnalyzerBinary/ClientAnalyzer
-    
-    echo "MDESupportTool installed at /tmp/XMDEClientAnalyzerBinary/ClientAnalyzer"
-    
-    ```
-
-#### Python client analyzer install script
-
-The following script performs the first six steps of the [Running the Python version of the Client Analyzer](run-analyzer-linux#run-the-python-based-client-analyzer). When complete, the XMDE Client Analyzer Python scripts are available from the `/tmp/XMDEClientAnalyzer` directory.
-
-- Create a bash file `InstallXMDEClientAnalyzer.sh` and paste the following content into it.
-
-    ```bash
-    #! /usr/bin/bash
-    
-    echo "Starting Client Analyzer Install Script. Running As:"
-    whoami
-    
-    echo "Getting XMDEClientAnalyzer.zip"
-    wget --quiet -O /tmp/XMDEClientAnalyzer.zip https://aka.ms/XMDEClientAnalyzer 
-    echo '07E6A7B89E28A78309D5B6F1E25E4CDFBA9CA141450E422D76441C03AD3477E7 /tmp/XMDEClientAnalyzer.zip' | sha256sum -c  
-    
-    echo "Unzipping XMDEClientAnalyzer.zip"
-    unzip -q /tmp/XMDEClientAnalyzer.zip -d /tmp/XMDEClientAnalyzer  
-    
-    echo "Setting execute permissions on mde_support_tool.sh script"
-    cd /tmp/XMDEClientAnalyzer 
-    chmod a+x mde_support_tool.sh  
-    
-    echo "Performing final support tool setup"
-    ./mde_support_tool.sh
-    
-    ```
-
-Tip
-
-Watch this video to learn more about endpoint settings: [Defender for Endpoint client analyzer endpoint settings](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Frw2xFjzphE)
-
-#### Run the client analyzer install scripts
-
-1. Initiate a [Live Response session](live-response#initiate-a-live-response-session-on-a-device) on the machine you want to investigate.
-2. Select **Upload file to library**.
-3. Select **Choose file**.
-4. Select the downloaded file named `InstallXMDEClientAnalyzer.sh`, and then select **Confirm**.
-5. While still in the LiveResponse session, use the following commands to install the analyzer:
-
-    ```console
-    run InstallXMDEClientAnalyzer.sh
-    ```
-
-### Run the XMDE client analyzer
-
-Live response doesn't support running the XMDE Client Analyzer or Python directly, so an execution script is necessary.
-
-Important
-
-The following scripts assume the XMDE Client Analyzer was installed using the same locations from the scripts mentioned earlier. If your organization chooses to install the scripts into a different location, then the scripts must be updated to align with your organization's chosen installation location.
-
-#### Script to execute the binary client analyzer
-
-The binary version of the client analyzer accepts command line parameters to perform different analysis tests. +7. Select **Uninstall**.

+### Block installation locally on an Arc-enabled server
+
+Use the Azure Connected Machine agent's local extension block list to prevent reinstallation on a specific server. Run these commands in an elevated PowerShell session on the Arc-enabled Windows server. These are `azcmagent` commands invoked from PowerShell, not Az PowerShell cmdlets.
+
+1. Add the Defender for SQL extension to the block list. The `--add` flag preserves existing entries.
+
+    ```powershell
+    $AgentPath = "$env:ProgramFiles\AzureConnectedMachineAgent\azcmagent.exe"
+    & $AgentPath config set extensions.blocklist `
+        "Microsoft.Azure.AzureDefenderForSQL/AdvancedThreatProtection.Windows" --add
+    if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "Couldn't add the Defender for SQL extension to the block list." }
+    ```
+2. Check that the block list includes `Microsoft.Azure.AzureDefenderForSQL/AdvancedThreatProtection.Windows`:
+
+    ```powershell
+    & $AgentPath config get extensions.blocklist
+    ```
+3. Return to the resource-level uninstall procedure and remove the extension. The block list doesn't uninstall an existing extension.
+
+If you manage an existing extension allow list instead, remove the Defender for SQL entry while retaining all other required entries. Don't clear the allow list or leave it empty as a way to block this extension: when neither list restricts installation, all extensions are allowed. The block list takes precedence if the extension remains in both lists.
+
+In agent monitor mode, you can't edit the local allow list or block list.
+

+
+### Block installation on an Azure VM
+
+Use Azure PowerShell to create a deny policy and assign it to the individual VM you want to exclude. The policy blocks only the Defender for SQL extension, identified by its publisher and type. It doesn't change restrictions on other extensions.
+
+The policy doesn't change the subscription-level Defender plan setting or turn off automatic provisioning. Installation attempts that match the policy are denied.
+
+1. Sign in and select the subscription that contains the VM:
+
+    ```powershell
+    Connect-AzAccount
+    Set-AzContext -SubscriptionId "<subscription-id>" -ErrorAction Stop
+    ```
+2. Create a policy definition that blocks the Defender for SQL extension on Azure VMs. The definition doesn't enforce the restriction until you assign it.
+
+    ```powershell
+    $PolicyRule = @'
+    {
+      "if": {
+        "allOf": [
+          { "field": "type", "equals": "Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/extensions" },
+          { "field": "Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/extensions/publisher", "equals": "Microsoft.Azure.AzureDefenderForSQL" },
+          { "field": "Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/extensions/type", "equals": "AdvancedThreatProtection.Windows" }
+        ]
+      },
+      "then": {
+        "effect": "deny"
+      }
+    }
+    '@
+    
+    $Definition = New-AzPolicyDefinition `
+        -Name "block-defender-sql-vm-extension" `
+        -DisplayName "Block Defender for SQL extension installation on Azure VMs" `
+        -Policy $PolicyRule `
+        -Mode All `
+        -ErrorAction Stop
+    ```
+3. Get the VM and assign the policy to its resource ID. Using the VM's ID limits the assignment to that VM, rather than its resource group or subscription.
+
+    ```powershell
+    $VM = Get-AzVM `
+        -ResourceGroupName "<resource-group>" `
+        -Name "<vm-name>" `
+        -ErrorAction Stop
+    
+    $Assignment = New-AzPolicyAssignment `
+        -Name "block-defender-sql" `
+        -Scope $VM.Id `

+        -EnforcementMode Default `

+    ```

+    ```powershell

+    ```

+5. Return to the resource-level uninstall procedure and remove the extension. Keep the assignment in place to block reinstallation. Remove the assignment before you enable protection again on that VM.

messageCenterItems.title: Microsoft Defender for Office 365: Move email messages to quarantine with a new remediation action
messageCenterItems.summary: Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Plan 2 introduces a "Move to Quarantine" remediation action, allowing admins to move suspicious emails from user mailboxes to Defender quarantine for safer investigation and management. Rollout begins late November 2026, with no action required but policy and role reviews recommended.
messageCenterItems.body:
Updated November 5, 2026: We have updated the timeline. Thank you for your patience. 

What and why

We are introducing Move to Quarantine, a new remediation action in Microsoft Defender for Office 365. It enables security teams to move potentially malicious email messages from users' mailboxes directly to Microsoft Defender quarantine. This provides a safer and more flexible way to contain suspicious messages that bypassed initial detection while preserving the ability to investigate, release, or permanently delete them later.

This capability is available with Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Plan 2, including eligible Microsoft 365 subscriptions that include Plan 2.

Rollout schedule

  • General Availability (Worldwide): Beginning in late November 2026 (previously early November) and expected to complete by mid-January 2027 (previously mid-December)

Impact on your organization

Who is affected

  • Organizations with Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Plan 2
  • Authorized security administrators who remediate email threats

Platforms and services

Microsoft Defender for Office 365, including:

  • Threat Explorer
  • Advanced Hunting
  • Custom detection rules for email results
  • Email entity and email summary experiences
  • Unified Action Center

What will happen

Authorized administrators will see a new Move to Quarantine remediation action.

When an administrator selects Move to Quarantine:

  • Selected email messages are removed from user-accessible mailbox locations and placed in Microsoft Defender quarantine.
  • Supported source locations include Inbox, Junk Email, Deleted Items, and recoverable soft-deleted locations.
  • Admins can select the quarantine policy when using the Move to quarantine action. The selected policy determines how end users can interact with the quarantined messages. By default, quarantined messages are accessible only to admins.
  • The remediation action and status are tracked in the Unified Action Center and related investigation experiences.
  • Quarantined messages are identified with the quarantine reason Admin triggered.
  • Authorized users can preview, release, or permanently delete quarantined messages according to the applicable quarantine policy.
  • Releasing a message from quarantine delivers the message to the user's Inbox.
  • The Search and Purge role is required to approve remediation actions.
  • If one or more messages cannot be moved, eligible messages continue processing and administrators can review the results for partial failures.

Screenshot 1 - Move to Quarantine option in the Take Action wizard:

 

Screenshot 2 - Admin-triggered message and action details displayed in Advanced Hunting:

 

The following existing functionality is unchanged:

  • Existing remediation actions, including Move to Junk, Move to Deleted Items, Soft delete, and Hard delete
  • Threat verdict assignments
  • Existing remediation approval workflows and permissions
  • Automated Investigation and Response (AIR) actions
  • Microsoft Graph API capabilities
  • Messages in unsupported locations, including hard-deleted messages and messages hosted in on-premises or external mailboxes

Action required and recommendations

No action is required to enable this capability.

We recommend that you:

  • Review your organization's quarantine policies.
  • Verify that appropriate administrators have the required Search and Purge role.
  • Update incident response playbooks and security operations procedures to include Move to Quarantine as a remediation option.
  • Update internal training and operational documentation as appropriate.
  • Inform security analysts and responders about the new containment action.

Learn more

Authorized users can later preview, release, or permanently delete quarantined messages according to the applicable quarantine policy.
